## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of crash‑consistent data structures in persistent memory, including proper ordering, flush/fence semantics, and recovery guarantees in a high‑throughput path.

## Key Concepts
- Persistent memory semantics and flush instructions (CLWB, CLFLUSHOPT, SFENCE)
- Two‑phase commit for durability
- Ring buffer invariants and recovery in power loss scenarios

## Code Example
```c
// Pseudo-code: writers publish after durable tail update
slot = tail & (N-1);
memcpy(slot_data(slot), payload, 64);
clwb(slot_data(slot));
clwb(&slot_seq(slot)); // update after data
sfence();
slot_seq(slot) = new_seq; // durable publish
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend to multiple producers and a multi‑consumer model with minimal contention?
- How would you validate durability guarantees under sudden power loss and after hot restarts?

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates the ability to design crash-safe concurrent data structures for non-volatile memory, assessing understanding of flush semantics, recovery mechanisms, and performance tradeoffs under contention.

## Key Concepts
- Persistent memory programming model and hardware semantics
- Write-ahead logging and flush primitives (CLWB, SFENCE)
- Per-slot version counters to prevent ABA problems
- Recovery procedures and WAL replay
- Memory ordering and cache-line alignment for performance

## Design Choice: Open Addressing
Linear probing with open addressing is preferred for NVRAM due to superior cache-line alignment, which minimizes unnecessary writes to persistent media, simplified recovery logic without traversing linked structures, and the elimination of pointer overhead inherent in chaining implementations.
